heard: Eyelashes freeze here. Cars are left running for hours. And around 500 people live here on purpose. Wab is already packed a suitcase.

So here's the real question. In a place this cold, why would anyone stop here at all? Part of the answer is hiding in the name. Oimaiakauen is usually explained as meaning water that does not freeze. Linguists argue about the exact roots, and some sources trace the word to the even language while others point to Saka. But the story told about this valley is the same. Nearby there were warm springs, water that stayed open through the winter. And if you move reindeer across a frozen landscape, open water is not a curiosity. It is the whole point. Wab, who has spent this entire trip complaining about frozen water bottles, suddenly understands. Water you can actually drink in the middle of winter is worth walking a very long way for.

So how cold is this cold, exactly? On the 6th of February, 1933, the weather station here recorded about minus 68 degrees Celsius. That is about minus 90 Fahrenheit. Guinness World Records lists it as minus 67.7. The World Meteorological Organization lists minus 67.8. So even the number itself comes with an argument. Either way, it is the lowest temperature on record for a place where people live all year. Well, almost. Far to the northwest, the town of Viennese Gai has its own reading from 1892 of about the same number. Some sources say the two towns share the record. Others treat the Viennese Gai reading as disputed. Rival towns. A tenth of a degree. More than a century of arguing. Wab finds this very relatable. Wab once argued with a fridge for an hour.

And then, the twist. Oymucon is not cold all year. Summers are short, but they can be properly warm. For a few weeks, the frozen valley turns green. By late June, daylight lasts more than 20 hours. In July 2010, the station recorded 34.6 degrees Celsius. That is about 94 Fahrenheit. Put the record low and the record high side by side. And the gap is roughly 102 degrees. Very few places on earth have record highs and lows that far apart. Wab, who packed nothing but fur, is suddenly optimistic again.

and the cold itself has become a reason to visit. Every spring, the district hosts a festival called the Pole of Cold, with events in villages including Oymucon and Tomtor. Its star is Kaizuke-Chan, the Sokka Lord of Cold, who reportedly has his own ice residence. In 2025, there was even a marathon here. In the cold, on purpose. A village that grew up around water that wouldn't freeze now welcomes visitors because of everything that does. Visitors come to stand next to the Pole of Cold Monument, take a photo and hurry back indoors. So let's add it all up. People stopped here because of water that would not freeze in a land where almost everything does. A stopping place became a village. A weather station gave it a famous reading, and that reading gave it a name the whole world knows. The highway that crosses the region carries a much darker history. And today, the families who live here stay for reasons that are easy to understand. Home, the school, the herds, the weather station, and, lately, visitors. The cold was never the reason to come. It was the price of staying.

So would Wobb move here. The springs are lovely. The summers are a genuine surprise. And the people of Oymucon have built a real home in one of the hardest places on the planet. But the winters here are long, dark and brutally cold, and Wobb packed for a weekend. The verdict is nope. This is a place for people who grew up with it, or who truly deeply love winter. Silence, clear skies, and a summer that feels earned. Wobb is unpacking. Slowly, with gloves on, Wobb will be following the thermometer from somewhere much warmer. So be honest, how long would you last out there?
